title: Let my people go (Exodus 5)
hookLine: the first demand, and Pharaoh makes the bricks harder to make

lines: TWO BROTHERS IN A THRONE ROOM.
cards: You know these four words even if you've never opened the book of Exodus. Enslaved people in America sang them in the fields: go down, Moses, tell old Pharaoh, let my people go.

People marching for freedom have painted them on signs. But the first time they were said, in the Torah, two brothers carried them into a throne room: Moses and Aaron, standing before the king of Egypt.

teach.b: They say: thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, "Let My people go, that they may hold a feast unto Me in the wilderness."
Pharaoh answers with a sneer: "Who is the LORD, that I should hearken unto His voice?" I don't know him, and I won't let Israel go. Then he does what every tyrant knows how to do.
That same day, he gives the taskmasters a new order: stop giving the people straw to make bricks. Let them gather it themselves, and keep the number of bricks the same.
They're lazy, he says; that's why they're crying, let us go. Make the work heavier, so they won't listen to lies. The people scatter all over Egypt looking for stubble.
They can't keep up. The Israelite foremen are beaten. And who do they blame?
Not Pharaoh. Moses and Aaron. You've made us stink in Pharaoh's eyes, they say; you've put a sword in their hand to kill us.
Moses turns to God, and he doesn't hold back. Why have you done evil to this people?

teach.h: WHY DID YOU EVER SEND ME?
teach.b: Why did you ever send me? Since I came, it's only gotten worse. The first try failed.
The people turned on their leader, and the leader turned to God with a complaint. And God doesn't scold him. God says: now you'll see what I'll do to Pharaoh.
The next chapter says the people couldn't even listen, because of their crushed spirit and hard labor. The Hebrew is kotzer ruach, shortness of breath.
That's what it feels like when it gets harder first.

how: At the Passover seder Jews retell the slavery in Egypt as their own story, and the words let my people go have been taken up by many freedom movements, including the African American spiritual Go Down, Moses.

o: shortness of breath: a crushed, worn-out spirit
God's own breath, blown into the first human
a long road: the journey out of Egypt

games.q: who said what — tap the pairs.
p: you've made us stink in his eyes
why did you ever send me?

s: after the first demand, Pharaoh eased the work
he took away the straw and kept the brick quota the same.
the Israelite foremen blamed Moses and Aaron
they said Moses had put a sword in the Egyptians' hands.
God answered: now you'll see what I'll do to Pharaoh.

games.q: you're Moses. your first demand has made everything worse. the people blame you. what do you do?
o: give up and go back to Midian.
turn to God and complain honestly.
games.why: he asks God, why have you done evil to this people? why did you send me? and God answers with what comes next.

practice: Think of something you tried recently that didn't work, or made things worse: a hard conversation, a new habit, a plan that fell apart. Let the voice that says why did I even start have its say, the way Moses did.
Then picture what a second try might look like; you don't have to do it today.

wordCard.voice: Kotzer ruach, shortness of breath, the Hebrew the Torah uses for the people who couldn't even listen, crushed by labor after the first demand made things harder.

orig.note: Hebrew: send out my people, let my people go.

carryVoice: Your line: it gets harder first. Even Moses asked why he'd been sent. Tomorrow, the plagues.
